quote: Roughly speaking, the half-silvered mirror rule is “multiply by 1 when the photon goes straight, and multiply by i when the photon turns at a right angle.”
content: The editors’ note corrects the phase; the larger omission is the normalization. A beam splitter is a unitary transformation, and a 50/50 splitter multiplies each output amplitude by 1/√2, so that the squared moduli sum to the input’s. The essay’s rule, 1 and i with no factor, sends an input of squared modulus 1 to two outputs of squared modulus 1 each, doubling the norm at every mirror; by the second beam splitter in Figure 2 the total is 4. The essay says only ratios matter, and for the predictions in these figures that is true. But the essay also says that this is “a computer program that resembled the underlying reality,” and the program it gives violates the one property, unitarity, that Collapse Postulates will later call the mark of every law in quantum mechanics except collapse. The point is small in the physics and large in the rhetoric: a sequence that condemns collapse as “the only non-unitary evolution in all of quantum mechanics” introduces its own dynamics with a non-unitary rule, and does not notice.

quote: A configuration is a variable in the program—you can think of it as a kind of memory location whose index is “a photon heading toward A”—and it’s out there in the territory.
content: The particle chosen to introduce configuration space is the one particle for which configuration space is least well defined. A “configuration” in the essay’s sense is a position basis state, and photons have no position operator in the ordinary sense; the standard result (Newton & Wigner (1949)) is that massless particles of nonzero spin are not localizable, and the question whether there is a photon wave function in position space at all has its own literature with no settled answer (Bialynicki-Birula, “Photon Wave Function,” Progress in Optics 36, 1996). Photon number is not conserved, photons are created and absorbed, and the “program” that resembles the reality of the experiments in Figures 1–3 is quantum electrodynamics on Fock space, not a complex number stored at the address “a photon heading toward A.” The essay is teaching nonrelativistic wave mechanics with a particle that wave mechanics does not describe, and the wavefunction-realist ontology it is building toward (“a perfectly normal cloud of complex amplitude in configuration space,” in Think Like Reality) is a picture whose relation to quantum field theory is an open problem for its own proponents (Wallace & Timpson (2010)). None of this affects the arithmetic of the figures. It affects the claim that the arithmetic is the territory.

quote: The ratio of these values is the ratio of the squared moduli of the amplitudes. But the reason for this is not something we are going to consider yet. Walk before you run.
content: The reason is never considered. The “magical squared-modulus-ratio reader” is the Born rule, and the promise that its connection to experimental frequencies will be explained “way up at the level of everyday life” is discharged in Many Worlds, One Best Guess with the sentence “there is no known reason for the Born probabilities.” Everything in the sequence that touches experiment passes through the magic tool, and the magic tool is the part of the theory the sequence cannot derive. This would be a fair place to say so, since the essay is careful about what is territory and what is not; instead the rule is presented as an instrument whose workings are postponed for pedagogical reasons, and the reader who reaches the end of the sequence discovers that the postponement was permanent. The same essay insists that “probability is in the mind to begin with”; the question of what the squared modulus is, if not a probability and not a fact about anyone’s mind, is the question Everettians have spent forty years on, and it is the question this paragraph declines to raise.
